discovery: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation
motivation: Before 1995 it was widely believed that decoherence made large-scale quantum computation physically impossible, because quantum states cannot be copied and errors are continuous. Shor (1995) and Steane (1996) showed independently that quantum information can be protected by encoding it redundantly across entangled qubits. Measuring error syndromes digitizes errors without disturbing the encoded state. Kitaev's topological codes, notably the toric and surface codes, and his anyonic model of fault-tolerant computation made protection a property of the physics of many-body systems. They also gave the local, high-threshold architecture that experiments now follow. These ideas define the goal of every quantum hardware platform. Recent experiments in superconducting circuits, trapped ions and neutral atoms have shown logical qubits whose errors fall as the code grows, and bosonic codes that pass the break-even point. They confirm that nature allows quantum coherence to be preserved indefinitely by active control.
